text: You're a train dispatcher in Halifax, Canada. It's December 6, 1917.
Out in the harbor, two ships bump into each other. And one is packed with explosives.
It catches fire, and the crew rows away, yelling that it's going to blow.
Nobody can hear them, and the ship drifts into a pier right by your station.
A sailor tells you to run, but there's a train with about 300 people due any minute.
So you stay, and tap out a warning. Hold up the train. Ammunition ship on fire. Goodbye, boys.
At 9:04 in the morning, the ship explodes, the biggest blast humans had ever made.
It flattens the north end of the city, and nearly 2,000 people die, including you.
But that train was held outside of town, and your warning went all the way down the line.
The next day, a blizzard buries the wrecked city, and thousands have no homes. But a train from Boston plows through the snow, packed with doctors and supplies.
Halifax never forgot. Every year, Nova Scotia still sends Boston a giant Christmas tree to say thank you.
Share this with someone who would stay at that telegraph, and subscribe for more true stories.
